name: Pratfall effect
statement: A blunder makes a competent person more likeable and a mediocre person less likeable, though only the second half reached significance in the 1966 experiment.
meaning: The claim is an interaction, not a rule about mistakes. Aronson, Willerman and Floyd predicted that a clumsy blunder would raise the attractiveness of a superior person and lower the attractiveness of a mediocre one. Their stated reasoning is that a great deal of ability can make a person seem too good, unapproachable and non-human, and that a blunder humanises him. Competence does the work in that account, so the blunder only helps someone the observer already rates highly. A version of the idea that says mistakes make people likeable has kept the memorable half and dropped the half that carries the prediction.

origin.who: Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman and Joanne Floyd
origin.note: A two-page report at pages 227 and 228 of volume 4, issue 6. Aronson was at the University of Texas, Willerman at the Social Science Research Council and Floyd at the University of Utah. The work was run at the University of Minnesota on two National Science Foundation grants, NSF GS 202 and NSF GS 750. The title is "The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness", and retellings routinely print "increased".

evidence: The 1966 paper was read in full from the publisher's PDF. Forty-eight male sophomores from an introductory psychology course at the University of Minnesota heard one of four tapes of a student trying out for the College Quiz Bowl team. The stimulus person answered 92% of 50 difficult questions or 30% of them, and on two of the four tapes he clumsily spilled a cup of coffee over himself near the end. Each rater then answered eight questions about him, marking each on a scale from -7 to +7, and the eight were summed into a composite attractiveness score. Mean scores were 30.2 for the superior blunderer, 20.8 for the superior person who did not blunder, -2.5 for the average blunderer and 17.8 for the average person who did not. Ability gave F = 14.90, df = 1/40, p < .001, and the ability by pratfall interaction gave F = 10.33, df = 1/40, p < .01. The pratfall on its own did nothing, and the paper reports no interviewer effects. Inside the average-ability pair the blunder cost 20.3 points, t = 3.15, p < .01. Inside the superior-ability pair it gained 9.4 points, t = 1.45, p < .18, which the paper states does not reach significance. A manipulation check on rated intelligence gave M = 5.73 against M = 0.83, t = 6.89, p < .005. The paper prints no effect size and no confidence interval, and the error term of 40 is what it gives rather than the 44 four cells of 48 would imply.

replication.headline: The paradigm was re-run through the 1970s and the later readable results do not line up, and the half of the effect everyone quotes missed significance in the original at p < .18.
replication.detail: Cunningham and Unverzagt had 192 students rate descriptions crossing competence with deviant behaviour. Their abstract at Crossref reports that deviance moved ratings more than competence did and that interactions of the two occurred rarely, which is the competent-transgressor interaction failing to appear. Maier, Lavrakas, Bentley and Parrella showed videotaped interactions in which a man blundered, a woman blundered, or nobody did, and found the blunderer derogated, most heavily by observers of the same sex, with 34 men and 34 women rating. Their design holds no competence manipulation. Kiesler and Goldberg crossed a blunder with the target's age and with opinion similarity in a two-by-two-by-two, then factor-analysed the attraction ratings into a socio-emotional and a task-related factor. Their abstract reports similarity as significant on both factors and reports no result for the blunder, and the full text was not obtained. Three closer repetitions from the same decade exist and could not be read. Helmreich, Aronson and LeFan brought in the observer's own self-esteem in 1970 and put "sometimes" in the title, Mettee and Wilkins crossed perceived ability with a humorous blunder in 1972, and Deaux tested sex differences in 1972. Feldman-Summers ran blunders under conditions of dependency in 1974. Modern work under the name is not a repetition. Mirnig and colleagues had 45 people talk to a NAO robot and then build Lego with it, the robot either committing eight errors or none. Likeability was 4.30 against 3.93 on a five-point scale, U = 340.00, z = 2.02, p = 0.044, r = 0.30, with 21 people in the error condition and 24 in the baseline. Anthropomorphism did not differ, p = 0.109, and ran lower for the faulty robot at 1.97 against 2.33. Nothing in that design manipulates competence, so it asks whether errors are liked, not whether competence changes what an error does.

study.cite: Cunningham, J., & Unverzagt, F. (1985). Effects of competence and deviance on person perception. Perceptual and Motor Skills, 60(2), 363-368.

limits: The three papers that repeat the original design with both halves of the interaction manipulated could not be obtained. Helmreich, Aronson and LeFan's 1970 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology carries no abstract at MEDLINE, Crossref, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar, and the publisher returned 403 to every request on 17 August 2026. The same holds for Mettee and Wilkins in 1972 and for Feldman-Summers in 1974. Deaux's 1972 paper ran in Representative Research in Social Psychology, has no DOI, and was not obtained; its citation here is taken from the reference list of Celik and colleagues. Kiesler and Goldberg, Maier and colleagues, and Cunningham and Unverzagt are described from their abstracts at Crossref and PubMed, because the SAGE full texts returned 403. No effect size is quoted for the original, because the paper prints none. Searches for repetitions covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar's 197 citing records read as titles, OpenAlex, the Internet Archive and general web search, on 17 August 2026.
misreadings: The popular form of the effect, that competent people become more likeable when they slip, is the half the original did not establish. The contrast that would show it ran to t = 1.45, p < .18. What the paper did establish is the interaction, and the drop for the mediocre blunderer, and its own abstract states that the attractiveness of a superior person is enhanced by a clumsy blunder without that qualification. The 1970 follow-up is skipped more often still. Two of the original authors put self-esteem in its title and "sometimes" in its headline claim, which fits badly with a rule stated without conditions. Marketing citations are looser again. The most recent paper carrying the name surveyed 234 Turkish Instagram users, kept from 364 respondents, who all read one scenario in which a travel influencer spills coffee. There is no condition without the spill, the authors list a two-by-two of expertise and pratfall as future work, and the study cannot show that the blunder changed anything. Robot studies are quoted the same way, as though a machine that people like more after it errs settles a question about people.
